title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol -- HTTP/1.1
summary: Describes HTTP/1.1, the application-level protocol for distributed, collaborative hypermedia information systems. It extends HTTP/1.0 with features such as persistent connections and virtual hosts. It was replaced by RFC 2616.

plainLanguage.summary: HTTP is how your browser asks a website for a page. Version 1.1 lets one connection fetch many things.

questions: what changed in http 1.1 from http 1.0
what is the host header in http
how do persistent connections work in http
subtitle: The first standard for HTTP/1.1: persistent connections, mandatory Host headers, caching rules and content negotiation.

tldr.problem: HTTP/1.0 did not properly handle hierarchical proxies, caching, persistent connections or virtual hosts, and many incomplete implementations were calling themselves HTTP/1.0.
tldr.mechanism: HTTP/1.1 keeps connections open by default, requires a Host header, defines precise cache expiration and validation rules, adds chunked transfer coding, and specifies content negotiation and new methods.
tldr.outcome: This Proposed Standard was obsoleted by RFC 2616, which is the revised HTTP/1.1 specification.

facts.label: Common methods
facts.value: 7 (OPTIONS, GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, DELETE, TRACE)

today: RFC 2068 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 2616, so it is a historical first edition of HTTP/1.1 and not the current definition.

sections.title: Why HTTP/1.1 Was Needed
sections.content:
The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is an application-level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypermedia information systems, and the RFC says it has been used by the World-Wide Web since 1990. HTTP/0.9 was a simple protocol for raw data transfer. HTTP/1.0, defined by RFC 1945, allowed MIME-like messages with metainformation about the data.

According to the RFC, HTTP/1.0 did not sufficiently take into consideration hierarchical proxies, caching, persistent connections and virtual hosts. Incompletely implemented applications calling themselves "HTTP/1.0" also made a version change necessary, so that two programs could learn each other's true capabilities. HTTP/1.1 therefore has more stringent requirements than HTTP/1.0.

The protocol uses a major.minor version number. The minor number goes up when features are added without changing how messages are parsed, and the major number goes up when the message format changes. Senders of these messages MUST use HTTP/1.1, which signals that they are at least conditionally compliant with the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The old version of HTTP made the web slow and confusing, like a shop where every customer had to leave and re-enter for each item. Version 1.1 wrote down clearer rules so everybody's shop and browser work the same way.

sections.title: Clients, Servers and Intermediaries
sections.content:
HTTP is a request/response protocol. A client sends a request containing a method, a URI and a protocol version, followed by a MIME-like message. The server answers with a status line, then a MIME-like message with server information and possibly an entity body.

Often there are programs between the two ends. The RFC names three kinds of intermediary: a proxy (a forwarding agent that may rewrite the request), a gateway (which receives requests as if it were the origin server and may translate to another protocol) and a tunnel (a blind relay, such as through a firewall). With three intermediaries, a message crosses four separate connections, and some HTTP options apply only to one connection while others apply along the whole chain.

Any party that is not a tunnel may keep a cache, which shortens the request chain when a stored response can be reused. Section 1.3 also fixes vocabulary used throughout: resource, entity, representation, variant, origin server, fresh, stale and validator.
sections.plainLanguage: When you ask for something, your request may pass through helpers on the way, like a school office passing a note along. A helper that already knows the answer can reply without bothering the far-away place.

sections.title: Request and Response Messages
sections.content:
Every message has a start line, zero or more header fields, an empty line and an optional message body. A request starts with a Request-Line: a method, the Request-URI and the HTTP version, separated by spaces. A response starts with a Status-Line: the HTTP version, a three-digit status code and a reason phrase. Header field names are case-insensitive, and methods are case-sensitive.

The Request-URI can be a lone asterisk (for requests about the server itself, such as OPTIONS *), an absolute URI (required when talking to a proxy) or an absolute path. In the common case of a path, the host name travels in a Host header. The path cannot be empty; if the URL has none it is sent as /.

The first digit of the status code gives its class: 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error and 5xx server error. The status code is for programs, while the reason phrase is for people and the client need not examine it.

The length of a message body is found by precedence rules in section 4.4. A message MUST NOT contain both a Content-Length header and the chunked transfer coding; if both arrive, the Content-Length is ignored. Every HTTP/1.1 application MUST be able to receive and decode chunked bodies, which send data as a series of size-prefixed chunks ended by a zero-sized chunk, so a server can start sending before it knows the total length.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message is like a letter: the first line says what you want or how it went, then come some labels, a blank line, and then the contents. Chunking lets you send a long story in small pieces when you do not know how long it will be yet.

sections.title: Persistent Connections and Pipelining
sections.content:
Before this RFC, a separate TCP connection was opened to fetch each URL, which added load on servers and congestion on the Internet. In HTTP/1.1, persistent connections are the default: unless otherwise indicated, a client may assume the server will keep the connection open. Either side signals the end with a Connection header containing the token close, and that request becomes the last on the connection. To stay persistent, every message needs a self-defined length rather than relying on the connection closing.

A client MAY pipeline requests, which means sending several without waiting for each response. The server MUST answer in the same order the requests arrived. Clients must be ready to resend if the server closes the connection before all responses arrive, and they SHOULD automatically retry only idempotent methods.

The RFC recommends limits to avoid congestion: a single-user client SHOULD keep at most 2 connections to any server or proxy, and a proxy SHOULD use up to 2*N connections to another server or proxy, where N is the number of simultaneously active users. A proxy MUST NOT establish a persistent connection with an HTTP/1.0 client.

Section 8.2 adds rules for sending large request bodies. A server can answer 100 (Continue) to tell the client to go on, or send an error status instead, and it MUST NOT perform the requested method if it returns an error.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of hanging up the phone after every question, you stay on the line and ask many questions in a row. You may even ask several at once, but the answers come back in the same order you asked.

sections.title: Methods
sections.content:
HTTP/1.1 defines seven common methods: OPTIONS, GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, DELETE and TRACE. The set can be extended, but GET and HEAD MUST be supported by all general-purpose servers. A server SHOULD return 405 (Method Not Allowed) for a known but disallowed method, and 501 (Not Implemented) for an unknown one.

  • GET retrieves whatever the Request-URI identifies. Adding headers such as If-Modified-Since makes it a conditional GET, and a Range header makes it a partial GET.
  • HEAD is the same as GET except that the server MUST NOT return a message body. It is often used to test links.
  • POST asks the server to accept the enclosed entity as a new subordinate of the resource, for uses such as annotation, posting to a bulletin board or submitting a form.
  • PUT stores the enclosed entity under the given URI. The URI names the entity itself, which is the difference from POST.
  • DELETE asks the origin server to delete the resource, though success is not guaranteed.
  • OPTIONS asks about communication options, and TRACE loops the request back to the client for diagnostics, with Max-Forwards limiting the chain.

GET and HEAD are considered safe because they should never have any significance other than retrieval. GET, HEAD, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, meaning N identical requests have the same side effects as one.
sections.plainLanguage: Methods are the verbs of the web: get me this, tell me about this, put this there, throw that away. Some verbs, like just looking, never change anything.

sections.title: Content Negotiation
sections.content:
A resource can have several representations, called variants, for example in different languages or formats. Content negotiation is how the best one is chosen. Any response with a body, including an error, may be negotiated.

In server-driven negotiation, an algorithm at the server picks, using request headers such as Accept, Accept-Language, Accept-Charset and Accept-Encoding. The RFC lists its drawbacks: the server cannot know what is truly best, sending preferences in every request is inefficient and can hurt privacy, it complicates servers, and it can limit what public caches can reuse. A server MUST send a Vary header in any cachable response that used server-driven negotiation.

In agent-driven negotiation, the user agent chooses from a list of alternatives the server provides, at the cost of a second request. HTTP/1.1 defines 300 (Multiple Choices) and 406 (Not Acceptable) for this. Transparent negotiation combines the two with a cache negotiating on the origin server's behalf, but this RFC defines no mechanism for it.
sections.plainLanguage: If a shop has the same book in English and French, either the shopkeeper guesses which you want from what you said, or hands you the list and you pick. Each way has good and bad points.

sections.title: Caching: Expiration and Validation
sections.content:
Caching is meant to eliminate the need to send requests in many cases, using expiration, and to eliminate the need to send full responses in many other cases, using validation. The overriding idea is semantic transparency: a cache should be invisible except for speed, and any weakening MUST be explicit and detectable, for example with a Warning header.

Servers set an expiry with the Expires header or the max-age directive of Cache-Control, and max-age takes priority. A response is fresh while its freshness lifetime exceeds its current age. Without an explicit time, caches may use a heuristic, which for a response with a Last-Modified time SHOULD be no more than some fraction of the interval since then, with 10% given as a typical setting. The Age header carries age estimates between caches.

When a stored response goes stale, the cache can validate it with a conditional request carrying a validator, either a Last-Modified date or an opaque entity tag (ETag). If the validator still matches, the server answers 304 (Not Modified) with no body. Otherwise it sends the full response. Entity tags may be strong or weak, and weak ones change only when the meaning of the entity changes.

Cache-Control directives such as no-cache, no-store, private, public, must-revalidate, max-stale and only-if-cached let servers and clients tighten or loosen the defaults. Responses to POST, PUT and TRACE are not cachable unless explicitly allowed, and a PUT or DELETE makes matching cache entries stale.
sections.plainLanguage: A cache is a lunchbox of answers you already got. A label says how long they stay fresh, and when they might be old you ask the cook, "Is this still good?" and the cook says "yes" without handing over a whole new lunch.

sections.title: Access Authentication
sections.content:
HTTP has a simple challenge-response mechanism. A server answers a request with 401 (Unauthorized) and a WWW-Authenticate header naming an authentication scheme and a realm. The realm, together with the server's root URL, defines the protection space. The client then retries with an Authorization header carrying credentials, which it may reuse for other requests in the same protection space.

The Basic scheme sends the user ID and password, joined by a colon and base64 encoded. A challenge looks like WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="WallyWorld". Digest authentication is not defined here but in RFC 2069. Proxies have their own pair, Proxy-Authenticate and Proxy-Authorization, while the user-agent headers must be forwarded untouched.
sections.plainLanguage: When a door is locked, the guard says "Who are you?" and you answer with your name and password. Basic is like saying the password out loud in a crowded room.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security section is a list of cautions rather than solutions. Its main warning is that Basic authentication is not a secure method of user authentication: the password travels as essentially clear text, so it SHOULD never be used without enhancements to protect sensitive or valuable information. It is also open to spoofing by counterfeit servers, which Digest authentication avoids, and users who reuse passwords make the risk worse.

When a server offers several authentication schemes, the RFC advises ordering them with the most secure first, and says clients should use the strongest scheme they understand. A man-in-the-middle could add a weak scheme or strip the choices and ask for Basic, so careful user agents could remember the strongest scheme a server ever asked for and warn before using a weaker one.

The section also covers abuse of server logs, which can reveal reading patterns, sensitive information in transit, attacks based on file and path names, personal information, privacy leakage from Accept headers, DNS spoofing and spoofing through Location headers.
sections.plainLanguage: The big warning is that Basic passwords can be read by anyone listening, like shouting your secret across a playground. Use something safer for anything important.

sections.title: Changes from HTTP/1.0
sections.content:
The appendix names the Host header as one of the most important changes. Older clients assumed one IP address per server. In HTTP/1.1, both clients and servers MUST support the Host request header, requests MUST include it, and a server MUST respond with 400 (Bad Request) if it is missing. Servers MUST also accept absolute URIs. Together these allow many web sites to share a single IP address.

Other changes include persistent connections by default, chunked transfer coding, the Cache-Control and entity-tag machinery, content negotiation, range requests and new methods such as OPTIONS and TRACE. An example request from the RFC shows the new minimum:

GET /pub/WWW/TheProject.html HTTP/1.1
Host: www.w3.org

Appendix 19.6 documents features, such as the PATCH method, that some implementations used but that could not be relied on to interoperate.
sections.plainLanguage: Now a browser must always say which website it wants. That lets one building house many different shops under a single street number.
